nuit_chaude.intro: A sleeping bag doesn't produce heat: it keeps in the heat you make. A few habits gain you several degrees.
etapes: Eat a fatty, hot meal in the evening, and keep a snack by you for the night: digesting warms you.
Go to the toilet before bed: your body won't spend energy keeping that liquid warm.
Get into bed warm, not chilled: walk or do a few squats before slipping into the sleeping bag.
Hot-water bottle: fill a metal or well-sealed bottle with hot water, wrap it in a sock and put it between your thighs or against your belly.
Keep a hat and dry socks just for the night. Never the damp socks of the day.
Don't breathe into the sleeping bag: the moisture in your breath wets it. Keep your nose and mouth outside and close the hood around them.
Add your dry clothes on top of you or inside the bag where you feel cold, and your pack under your feet to insulate from the ground.
attention: A hot-water bottle that's too hot against the skin can burn you while you sleep: always wrap it.
If you shiver uncontrollably or become clumsy, it's the start of hypothermia: see the dedicated sheet.
nuit_chaude.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

condensation.intro: In the morning, the inside of the tarp is streaming and the sleeping bag is damp? That's condensation: your breath and moist air turning into water on the cold fabric.
etapes: Avoid valley bottoms, wet meadows and the immediate edge of the water: that's where the air is dampest and the dew heaviest.
Keep the shelter open and well ventilated: a tarp raised a few centimetres on one side keeps the air moving.
Don't dry wet clothes under the shelter overnight.
If the fabric is streaming, wipe it with a cloth before it drips.
In the morning, turn the sleeping bag inside out and let it dry in the sun or air during breakfast.
Pack the wet tarp separately, in an outside bag, and dry it at the first sunny break.
condensation.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

camp_pluie.titre: Setting up camp in the rain
camp_pluie.intro: Arriving at the bivouac in a downpour is when everything can get wet. A method to keep the essentials dry.
etapes: Pack your bag the day before in reverse order of setting up: tarp and cord at the top, sleeping bag right at the bottom in a dry bag.
Put the roof up first (see “Pitching your tarp in rain and wind”).
Under the roof, lay the groundsheet or a layer of leaves, then and only then the mat and sleeping bag.
Change immediately: take off wet clothes and put on the dry outfit kept for the night.
Keep the wet clothes for the next day, rolled in a bag: you'll put them back on to walk, and the dry outfit will stay dry.
Have a hot drink and eat: a cold, hungry body warms up badly.
camp_pluie.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

peche_regles.intro: Fishing without a licence in a public river is an offence. Before casting a line, a few checks are needed.
etapes: Wallonia: a fishing licence is compulsory in public rivers, canals and lakes. It can only be bought online (permisdepeche.be) and is valid until 31 December. A 14-day “tourist” licence exists for visitors.
Some stretches also require a club card or the riverbank owner's permission.
Each species has its open seasons, minimum size and sometimes a daily quota: check the rules of the Maison wallonne de la Pêche (maisondelapeche.be).
Species to release in Wallonia: eel, salmon, and all protected species (bullhead, noble crayfish…).
Forbidden: fishing in marked spawning areas, using whole animals (frogs, chicks, mice) as bait, or live bait not on the authorised list.
France: you need a fishing card from an approved association (AAPPMA), bought online or from a dealer. Other countries have similar rules.
Fish traps, nets, ledger lines left unattended or hand fishing are forbidden for amateur anglers in most cases.
attention: In real distress (lost for several days, without food), survival comes before the rules. But a healthy person lasts weeks without eating: water, warmth and signalling remain the priorities.
peche_regles.source: Wallonia's public fishing rules (SPW, Maison wallonne de la Pêche), INBO opinion on pollutants in freshwater fish, standard naturalist knowledge; written for Bivaska

poisson_pollution.intro: Many rivers in Western Europe still contain pollutants that build up in fish: PCBs, dioxins, mercury, PFAS. Cooking doesn't destroy them.
etapes: The most contaminated: eel (never eat it), large bottom-feeders (carp, catfish, barbel) and old large predators (pike, zander).
The least contaminated: young, small, lean fish, and trout from upstream brooks, far from towns and industry.
Avoid fishing to eat downstream of large towns, industrial areas, sewage works or in water with an abnormal smell or colour.
Pollutants lodge mainly in fat: remove the skin, the belly fat and the brown line along the sides, and don't eat the liver or roe.
Cook on a grill or in the oven so the fat drains away, rather than in a sauce or soup.
Limit yourself to a meal of wild fish now and then. Pregnant women and children should avoid river fish.
Never eat a fish found dead, nor a fish caught in an area where a ban on taking fish is posted.
attention: A Flemish study (INBO) concludes that a large share of freshwater fish in Flanders still exceeds consumption limits, and that anglers who eat their catch have high levels of pollutants in their blood.
poisson_pollution.source: Wallonia's public fishing rules (SPW, Maison wallonne de la Pêche), INBO opinion on pollutants in freshwater fish, standard naturalist knowledge; written for Bivaska

poisson_frais.intro: Without a fridge, fish spoils within hours, even faster in hot weather. A few signs don't lie.
etapes: Bulging, bright, clear eyes. Sunken, dull or milky eyes: fish too old.
Bright red, moist gills. Brown, grey or slimy: throw it away.
Firm flesh: a finger leaves no mark. Soft flesh that keeps the dent is no longer good.
A light smell of water or seaweed. A strong, sour or ammonia smell: throw it away.
Be wary of a sick fish: sores, swellings, frayed fins, abnormal swimming, strange colour.
Once caught, kill it straight away, gut it, and eat it within hours, or dry or smoke it (sheet “Preparing and cooking a fish”).
poisson_frais.source: Wallonia's public fishing rules (SPW, Maison wallonne de la Pêche), INBO opinion on pollutants in freshwater fish, standard naturalist knowledge; written for Bivaska

poisson_preparer.intro: Killed properly, gutted straight away and cooked through: that's what makes a river fish safe and good.
etapes: Kill quickly: a sharp blow on top of the head with a stick, just behind the eyes. It's more humane, and the flesh keeps better.
Bleed: cut the gills on one side and let it drain for a few minutes.
Scale: scrape with the back of the blade, from tail to head. Not needed for trout.
Gut: cut open the belly from the vent to the head, remove all the guts and scrape out the dark line along the backbone (the kidney). Never keep barbel roe.
Do this away from the water and the camp, and bury the remains: they attract animals.
Cook through: the flesh must become opaque and come away easily from the bone. On a spit, wrapped in leaves or on a hot stone (sheet “Cooking without utensils”).
To keep it longer: cut into thin strips and dry and smoke them for several hours over a gentle, smoky fire.
attention: Never eat freshwater fish raw, marinated or barely cooked: it can transmit parasitic worms (fish tapeworm, liver fluke). Only thorough cooking, or long freezing at -20 °C, destroys them.
poisson_preparer.source: Wallonia's public fishing rules (SPW, Maison wallonne de la Pêche), INBO opinion on pollutants in freshwater fish, standard naturalist knowledge; written for Bivaska

peche_survie.intro: In real distress, an improvised line can provide food. But fishing takes time and patience: it's never priority number one.
etapes: Hook: a bent safety pin, a hawthorn or blackthorn spine tied onto a small stick, or a “gorge hook”: a small stick pointed at both ends, tied in the middle, which the fish swallows lengthwise.
Can-tab hook: cut the ring-pull of a can on one side of the ring, bend the cut part into a hook and sharpen the point on a stone. The other ring is for tying on the line.
Line: thin cord, dental floss, braided nettle fibres or the inner threads of paracord.
Bait: earthworms (under stones, logs, in damp soil), insect larvae under dead bark or river stones, grasshoppers. On site, the stomach of a first fish gives the ideal bait.
Where: in the eddies behind rocks, under undercut banks, at the edge of weed beds, near submerged wood, at the bottom of rapids.
When: at dawn and dusk, when fish feed. In overcast weather, they also bite during the day.
Stay discreet: approach slowly, without casting a shadow on the water, without vibrations on the bank.
Check the line often and never leave an abandoned line in the water: it kills fish and birds.
attention: Outside a real emergency, these methods are forbidden: see “Fishing: what the law says”.
Fishing often costs more energy than it brings in. Water, shelter, fire and signalling come first.
peche_survie.source: Wallonia's public fishing rules (SPW, Maison wallonne de la Pêche), INBO opinion on pollutants in freshwater fish, standard naturalist knowledge; written for Bivaska

piqure_vive.intro: An immediate, violent pain in the foot after walking in the sand at low tide: it's almost always a weever. The venom is destroyed by heat.
etapes: Get out of the water and sit down calmly.
Immerse the stung area in very hot water, around 45 °C, for at least 15 to 30 minutes, or until the pain eases. Top up with hot water as you go.
Test the temperature with your unaffected hand or someone else's: the stung area is numb and could get burnt without you feeling it.
Without hot water: a hairdryer or a hot compress, at a safe distance from the skin.
Remove any visible bits of spine with tweezers, then clean and disinfect.
The pain usually eases within a few hours and disappears in one to two days.
attention: Don't cut, suck or urinate on it, and don't apply a tourniquet.
Feeling faint, severe dizziness, nausea, difficulty breathing or spreading swelling: see a doctor or call 112.
piqure_vive.source: Wallonia's public fishing rules (SPW, Maison wallonne de la Pêche), INBO opinion on pollutants in freshwater fish, standard naturalist knowledge; written for Bivaska

blessure_poisson.titre: Injuries from fish spines and teeth
blessure_poisson.intro: Perch, zander or catfish spines, pike teeth: the small wounds made by a fish get infected easily, because they're deep and dirty.
etapes: Let the wound bleed a little to help it clean itself.
Rinse for a long time with drinking water, then soap if possible.
Remove any visible piece of spine or tooth with tweezers.
Disinfect and cover with a clean dressing.
Very painful catfish sting: very hot water also helps (as for a weever).
Watch the wound for several days (sheet “Caring for a wound over several days”).
attention: Spreading redness, heat, swelling, a red streak up the arm or fever: infection, see a doctor quickly.
Check that your tetanus vaccination is up to date.
blessure_poisson.source: Wallonia's public fishing rules (SPW, Maison wallonne de la Pêche), INBO opinion on pollutants in freshwater fish, standard naturalist knowledge; written for Bivaska

bache_montages.titre: Ten ways to pitch a tarp
bache_montages.intro: With a 3 × 3 m square tarp, a ridgeline and a few pegs, you can pitch about ten different shelters. The right one depends on the wind, the rain and the number of people.
etapes: A-frame: the tarp draped over a low cord, both edges pegged to the ground. The classic against rain (dedicated sheet).
Closed A-frame with floor: the same, with the edges folded under you to make a floor. When the ground is wet (dedicated sheet).
Lean-to: one edge on the cord, the other pegged to the ground on the wind side. Open view, ideal in calm weather (dedicated sheet).
Envelope: a lean-to whose bottom is folded inwards to form a floor. Open on one side only.
Windbreak corner: a steeply angled lean-to with one side folded down to the ground facing the wind. Closed to the wind on two sides.
Plough point: a single corner tied high to a tree, the other three on the ground. Very good in wind for one person (dedicated sheet).
Arrowhead: one corner tied high, the tarp stretched in an A along a cord that runs down to the ground behind. High at the entrance, low at the feet, very stable.
Forest tent: one corner raised by a stick at the front, the two side corners pegged to the ground and the last one pulled out behind. A small, closed pyramid tent.
Flat roof: all four corners tied high to trees or sticks, one corner lower so water runs off. For cooking or resting out of the rain.
Walking poles: two poles set to 1.1 m hold up the front of the cord, the back is pegged to the ground. For camping where there are no trees.
attention: Always a slope on the roof: a tarp pitched flat makes a pocket of water that ends up coming through.
Practise at home: you don't discover a pitch in the rain and the dark.
bache_montages.source: Standard bivouac and survival know-how, written for Bivaska

sac_charger.intro: A well-packed bag weighs the same, but feels much lighter: the centre of gravity stays close to your back and the bag no longer pulls you backwards.
etapes: Right at the bottom: the sleeping bag, in a dry bag. You only need it at camp, and it cushions everything else.
In the centre, against your back, between the shoulder blades: the heaviest things (water, food, stove, cookset).
Around the heavy items: medium-weight things (spare clothes, tent or tarp), to wedge everything in.
At the top and towards the outside: light things and what you use during the day (rain jacket, fleece, first-aid kit).
In the lid and hip-belt pockets: map, compass, head torch, knife, snacks, phone, whistle. Everything that must come out without opening the bag.
Balance left and right, then tighten the compression straps so nothing moves.
Adjustment: the weight rests on your hips. Tighten the hip belt on your hip bones, then the shoulder straps, then the load lifters.
attention: Waterproof liner essential: a big bin bag inside the backpack keeps everything dry, even in a thunderstorm.
sac_charger.source: Standard bivouac and survival know-how, written for Bivaska

filtre_meche.intro: A strip of cloth dipped in cloudy water, the other end hanging into a lower container: the water climbs through the fibres and drips out, much clearer. Spectacular, but be careful about what it really does.
etapes: Put the container of dirty water higher than the clean container (on a stone).
Take a strip of clean cotton cloth, or a sock, thoroughly wet.
Dip one end to the bottom of the dirty water, run the cloth over the rim and let the other end hang into the clean container, lower than the dirty water.
Wait: the water slowly migrates through the fibres and drips. Allow several hours for half a litre.
Then boil the water you get for at least 1 minute (sheet “Making water safe to drink”).
attention: This filter removes mud and particles, but NOT bacteria, viruses and parasites: clear water can make you very ill. Always boil it afterwards.
Very slow: useful for clearing muddy water before boiling it, not for drinking quickly.
filtre_meche.source: Standard bivouac and survival know-how, written for Bivaska

nasse_bouteille.intro: A plastic bottle cut and turned inside out becomes a trap for small fish and crayfish: they get in through the neck and can't find the way out.
etapes: Cut a large bottle a third of the way down, just below the shoulder.
Remove the cap, turn the top part upside down and push it into the body, neck facing inwards.
Fix the two parts together with string threaded through small holes, or with thorns.
Pierce a few small holes so water flows through and the bottle sinks.
Put bait inside (worms, crumbs, fish scraps) and a small stone to weigh it down.
Set it on the bottom, neck facing the current, tied to the bank with string. Check it every hour or two.
attention: A method forbidden to amateur anglers in Wallonia, France and most European countries. Keep it for a real emergency.
Release protected species immediately. American crayfish must never be transported alive.
nasse_bouteille.source: Standard bivouac and survival know-how, written for Bivaska

ligne_ressort.intro: A bent flexible branch acts as a spring: when a fish pulls on the bait, it releases a small trigger and the branch springs up, setting the hook.
etapes: Choose a flexible dead branch or a young shoot already bent over the water. Don't cut anything living if you can avoid it.
Carve two pegs with a notch each: one is driven into the bank, the other (the trigger) hooks underneath it, notch against notch.
Tie the line to the end of the branch, bend the branch down and hook it onto the trigger.
Attach the line with the hook and bait to the trigger: when the fish pulls, the notches release and the branch springs up.
Set the depth of the bait, then move away and watch from a distance.
attention: A method forbidden to amateur anglers in Wallonia, France and most European countries. Keep it for a real emergency.
A branch that springs back can whip your face: never lean over it while setting it.
Never leave a set line unattended, and dismantle it when you leave.
ligne_ressort.source: Standard bivouac and survival know-how, written for Bivaska

ps_echarpe.intro: For an injury to the hand, wrist, arm or shoulder: the sling supports the arm, eases the pain and often lets you keep walking.
etapes: Take a square of cloth at least 1 m across (scarf, cut-up T-shirt, thin tarp) and fold it into a triangle.
Slide the triangle between the chest and the injured arm, the point towards the elbow on the injured side and one end going over the uninjured shoulder.
Gently bend the injured arm at a right angle across the chest, the wrist a little higher than the elbow.
Bring the other end of the triangle up over the forearm to the shoulder on the injured side.
Tie the two ends at the side of the neck, not on the back of the neck, with a little padding under the knot.
Close the point at the elbow with a pin or a knot, so the arm doesn't slip out.
For more immobilisation, add a wide band around the chest, over the arm.
isole: Without cloth: turn up the bottom of your jacket over the forearm and pin it, or slip your hand inside the zipped jacket.
A pack strap or a belt passed around the neck and the wrist makes a simple sling.
Check every hour that the fingers stay warm, pink and have feeling, and loosen if it swells.
With a good sling, you can often keep walking slowly: lighten the pack and carry it on the other side.
alerte: Fingers cold, pale, bluish or numb
ps_echarpe.source: Standard bivouac and survival know-how, written for Bivaska
